title: Development Economics
summary: Learn how countries reduce poverty and raise living standards: measuring development, economic growth and productivity, poverty traps and inequality, education and health, agriculture and structural change, and institutions, aid, trade and finance.
audience: Economics and development students, policy-makers, NGO staff and engaged citizens

body.p: Development economics studies how low- and middle-income countries can raise living standards, reduce poverty and expand people's freedoms and opportunities. Development is about more than income: health, education, security, voice and the environment all matter.

list: GDP (gross domestic product) is the value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. A country with a GDP of $450 billion and 50 million people has GDP per person of $9000.
Purchasing power parity (PPP) adjusts for different price levels, because a dollar buys more in some countries than others.
Real growth removes inflation: nominal growth of 9% with 6% inflation is roughly 3% real growth.
Per-person growth subtracts population growth: 5% GDP growth with 2.7% population growth is about 2.3% per person.

body.p: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education and income. Multidimensional poverty indices count deprivations in health, education and living standards. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set 17 global goals for 2030, from ending poverty to climate action.

body.tip: Always check whether a growth figure is nominal or real, and total or per person; the difference is often large.

body.p: Sustained growth is the main way countries have reduced mass poverty. Growth comes from more inputs (labour and capital) and, above all, from producing more with them (productivity).

The rule of 70 estimates doubling time: income growing 7% a year doubles in about 10 years; at 2% it takes about 35 years. Growing 2.3% a year per person for 30 years almost doubles income (1.023³⁰ is about 1.98). Small differences in growth rates compound into huge differences over decades.

list: Physical capital: machines, roads, power and ports.
Human capital: education, skills and health.
Technology and innovation, including adopting existing technologies.
Institutions: secure property rights, rule of law, effective government and low corruption.
Structural transformation: moving workers from low-productivity activities (such as subsistence farming) to higher-productivity ones (manufacturing, modern services and commercial farming).

body.p: Solow's growth model shows that investment alone eventually runs into diminishing returns; long-run growth in income per person depends on technological progress and productivity.

body.tip: When you hear a growth target, ask what will raise productivity, not only what will raise spending.

body.p: Extreme poverty is measured against an international poverty line set by the World Bank at a few dollars a day in PPP terms, updated periodically; countries also set national poverty lines. Global extreme poverty fell sharply over recent decades, mainly through growth in East and South Asia, while a growing share of the world's extreme poor live in sub-Saharan Africa.

list: Nutrition: poorly nourished workers are less productive, earning too little to eat well.
Health: disease reduces income and schooling.
Credit: without collateral, the poor cannot borrow to invest.
Geography: remote, landlocked or disease-prone areas face higher costs.
Risk: shocks such as droughts push households to sell assets, keeping them poor.

body.p: Inequality affects how much growth reduces poverty. Measures include the Gini coefficient and income shares. Policies that reduce inequality include quality public education and health, progressive taxation, social protection such as cash transfers, and fair access to land and finance.

body.tip: Look at both levels and distribution: average income can rise while the poorest fall behind.

body.p: People are the most important resource of any economy. Investments in education and health raise productivity and wellbeing.

Each extra year of schooling is associated with higher earnings, often estimated at around 8 to 10% a year; four extra years at 8% suggests earnings about 32% higher (roughly, ignoring compounding). But schooling is not the same as learning: many children in school do not reach basic reading and maths levels. Effective policies include teaching at the right level, structured lessons, and better-supported teachers.

list: Childhood health and nutrition affect lifelong earnings and learning.
Vaccines, bed nets, deworming and clean water are among the most cost-effective investments known.
Health insurance and free basic care protect households from catastrophic spending.

body.p: Randomised controlled trials, recognised by the 2019 Nobel Prize in Economics (Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer), test which interventions work. For example, if a programme raises reading scores for 60% of pupils, and half of those gains last a year later, 30% show lasting improvement.

body.tip: Ask for evidence of impact and cost per outcome when comparing development programmes.

body.p: In many low-income countries, most people work in agriculture, often with low productivity. Raising farm productivity frees labour and raises incomes.

list: Improved seeds, fertiliser, irrigation and extension services raise yields.
Secure land rights encourage investment.
Roads, storage and market access reduce post-harvest losses and raise farm-gate prices.
Agro-processing adds value and creates jobs.

body.p: East Asian economies grew through export-oriented manufacturing. Some African economies are pursuing manufacturing through special economic zones and regional markets under the African Continental Free Trade Area. Others are growing through services such as ICT, finance and tourism. Debates continue about the best path, including concerns about "premature deindustrialisation" and the role of industrial policy.
Much employment is informal: small businesses and self-employment without contracts or social protection. Policies aim to raise productivity and protections without stifling enterprise.

body.tip: Look at where workers are moving, from which sectors to which; it reveals the shape of structural change.

body.p: Economists such as Acemoglu and Robinson argue that inclusive institutions, which protect rights and spread opportunity, drive long-run prosperity, while extractive institutions concentrate power and wealth. Colonial histories shaped many institutions, and reforms such as independent courts, accountable budgets and anti-corruption agencies aim to improve them.

Development aid funds health, education, infrastructure and humanitarian relief. Supporters point to successes such as vaccination and disease programmes; critics warn of dependency, poor targeting and weakened accountability. Evidence suggests aid works better when aligned with country priorities, predictable and rigorously evaluated.

list: Trade allows specialisation and access to larger markets; regional integration can help small economies.
Commodity dependence exposes countries to price swings; diversification reduces risk.
Foreign direct investment brings capital and technology; terms and governance matter.
Remittances from migrants are large and stable sources of income for many households.
Mobile money and financial inclusion help households save, borrow and manage risk.

body.tip: Compare development strategies by their evidence and trade-offs, not by ideology.
